description:
FOUND s491/s492 (Fable) by the everyday-Perl battery (#1994, idiom 36); probed vs perl 5.40.3, main 268d7e00: ~/pcl-agent-scratch/s492/probes/alarm1.pl
  1  eval { local $SIG{ALRM} = sub { die "timeout\n" }; alarm 1; <busy loop with 4-arg select> }     caught: timeout on both      RIGHT
  2  the same with `sleep 5` inside the eval                                                          caught: timeout2 on both     RIGHT
  3  local $SIG{ALRM} = sub { $got++ }; alarm 1; my $slept = sleep 4;     perl: handler ran, sleep returned after ~1 s with $slept = 1      PCL: handler ran, sleep took the full 4 s, $slept = 4
  4  alarm 10; my $rem = alarm 0;                                                                      9 or 10 on both              RIGHT
So signals are delivered and handlers run DURING the sleep; only the early return is missing.  WHERE: `p-sleep` (cl/pcl-runtime.lisp) -- SBCL's `sleep` resumes after an interrupt.  FIX SHAPE: p-sleep records that a perl-level signal handler ran during it (the runtime's handler trampoline sets a flag / bumps a counter) and returns the elapsed whole seconds when one did -- the same for 4-arg `select` with a timeout (perl: returns -1/EINTR; probe).  #1992 (the Time::HiRes shim) REWRITES p-sleep for fractional seconds -- do this in the same edit, not as a second pass over the function.  Low priority on its own.  BAR: `cl/` => full sweep + companion op/sleep.t op/alarm.t op/sigdispatch.t legs; guard row with a 1 s alarm and a RANGE assertion.


=== DONE (s492c, 2026-09-21, Opus) ===
Done in the same edit as #1992's p-sleep rewrite, as the task asked.

perl's `sleep` returns early when a signal handler ran during it.  SBCL's
`sleep` resumes after an interrupt, so the early return is a NON-LOCAL EXIT
from the handler: `%p-sleep-seconds` publishes a catch tag in
`*p-sleep-wakeup*` for the duration of the sleep, and the SIGALRM trampoline
throws to it after the Perl handler RETURNS (a handler that dies already
unwinds).  Nothing is polled, and a program that never sleeps pays nothing.

`p-sleep` returns the whole seconds actually slept, so `alarm 1; my $s =
sleep 4` is 1, as in perl.  Probe alarm1.pl: all four rows identical to perl
(the classic die-in-handler timeout idiom included).  Guard rows 11-12 of
Pl/t/time-hires-01.t.

NOT COVERED, and it is the reason only ALRM can end a sleep today: PCL
installs a Unix handler for SIGALRM only, so `$SIG{TERM}`/`$SIG{CHLD}` etc.
never run at all (task #2094's second half).  When they do, they must throw to
the same tag.


=== DONE (s492c) ===
SHIPPED s492c member 1 (0684b77e), inside the p-sleep rewrite.  perl's sleep
RETURNS EARLY when a signal handler ran during it; SBCL's resumes, so a
sleeping thread publishes a catch tag (*p-sleep-wakeup*) and the SIGALRM
trampoline throws to it after the Perl handler returns.  Nothing is polled and
a program that never sleeps pays nothing.
subject: EDGE (pre-existing): `sleep` is NOT interrupted by a signal whose handler RETURNS -- perl's sleep returns early with the seconds slept; PCL runs the handler and then sleeps the FULL remaining time (a daemon's `while (!$done) { sleep 60 }` sees its TERM/CHLD flag up to a minute late); the classic die-in-handler timeout idiom is RIGHT
